subject: preparedness-v2

object.value: Whether Version 2’s governance arrangements permit OpenAI Leadership to deploy High-capability models without sufficient safeguards

statement: Preparedness Framework v2’s governance arrangements permit OpenAI Leadership to deploy models with High capabilities without safeguards that sufficiently minimize their associated risks.

time.note: Dated by the edition. OpenAI’s announcement was published with it on 2025-04-15 and the ChatGPT agent system card on 2025-07-17; Coggins et al. submitted v1 of their analysis on 2025-09-29 and revised it as v2 on 2025-10-13.

qualification: Contested assessment of the policy’s permissiveness, not a finding that OpenAI deployed a model without safeguards, a legal ruling or a guarantee of compliance. Coggins et al. (arXiv:2509.24394; v1 2025-09-29, v2 2025-10-13) read the framework’s governance arrangements as letting OpenAI Leadership, the CEO or a person designated by them, approve or reject the Safety Advisory Group’s recommendations and so deploy even more dangerous capabilities, especially if other developers do so. OpenAI’s announcement of Version 2 states that covered systems reaching High capability must have safeguards that sufficiently minimize the associated risk of severe harm before they are deployed, and its ChatGPT agent system card describes the framework as committing it to such safeguards; both predate the analysis and are not replies to it. The record does not decide whether leadership’s authority over the recommendations defeats that stated requirement. The paper’s framework-wide conclusion and OpenAI’s comparison of Version 2 with its predecessor are context. The rule’s own wording is recorded in prov-preparedness-v2-high-deployment-restriction.

subject: anthropic

object.value: Whether Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust is independent enough of stockholders to exercise effective public-interest oversight of Anthropic in practice

statement: Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust has sufficient independence from stockholders to exercise effective public-interest oversight of Anthropic in practice.

time.note: The question is not tied to one date: it concerns the Trust under the rights recorded on this page, which phase in from 6 September 2023. The cited passages were published from 19 September 2023 to 23 July 2026 (the Transparency Hub version last updated that day); those are source dates, not the period of the question.

qualification: The unresolved question is whether the Trust can exercise effective public-interest oversight when stockholder preferences conflict with that oversight. Anthropic describes financially disinterested Trustees, an intended independent design and a checking role; its Transparency Hub says the Trust’s authority to elect directors helps insulate the mission from short-term commercial and shareholder pressures, and its April 2026 announcement says Trust-appointed directors then formed a board majority. Appointment power is distinct from independence against removal. Stein-Perlman’s 2024 analysis tentatively identifies possible stockholder subordination under incompletely disclosed failsafe terms. Fried and Reiter describe partial investor insulation and favour constraints on guardian overreach; they do not simply deny an effective checking role. Outside counsel describe the arrangement’s accountability and amendment mechanisms. Source dates and subsequent phase-in must be distinguished. The inspected public descriptions do not settle practical effectiveness; no side or legal conclusion is adopted.

subject: openai-group-pbc

object.value: Whether the OpenAI Foundation can exercise effective mission-directed control over OpenAI Group PBC in practice after the October 2025 recapitalization

statement: Following the October 2025 recapitalization, the OpenAI Foundation can exercise effective mission-directed control over OpenAI Group PBC in practice.

time.note: Dated by the recapitalization whose control arrangements the question concerns (the certificate filed and the Delaware Attorney General’s letter of 28 October 2025). The date does not bound a period of effective control, and no end is recorded. The cited passages were published from 28 October 2025 to 11 May 2026 (OpenAI’s structure page is undated); those are source dates, not the period of the question.

qualification: Effective control here concerns the Foundation’s ability to enforce its mission through its retained governance powers when commercial interests or Group management resist. OpenAI asserts continuing control; formal rights are documented separately. Bret Taylor’s announcement for OpenAI’s board says the recapitalization keeps the mission at the center and maintains the strongest representation of mission-focused governance in the industry. Not For Private Gain recognises improvements over the abandoned proposal while judging control weaker than under the former structure and identifying conditional risks to effective exercise. CalMatters reports critics’ concerns about possible commercial predominance. Fried and Reiter describe the Foundation’s appointment, veto and safety-blocking powers as substantial authority over investors and argue that guardians may do too much as well as too little. The Delaware Attorney General’s non-objection is conditional on representations. These sources do not settle practical effectiveness, and no legal conclusion or side is adopted.

subject: openai-group-pbc-certificate-2025

object.value: Class N stock’s director-election rights while held by OpenAI Foundation

statement: The certificate states that, so long as Class N Common Stock is issued, outstanding and held directly or indirectly by OpenAI Foundation, holders of Class A Common Stock may not vote in director elections. Where Class B Common Stock is also outstanding, the Class N shares carry the greater of 66.67% of the voting power or the share of Class N and Class B stock that the Foundation’s Class N shares represent, and no director-election quorum exists without the Class N holder.

time.note: The certificate’s filing date, recorded as its publication date.

qualification: What the filed text says. The certificate authorises one share of Class N Common Stock (Section IV.1(a)). The provision conditions its effect on the Foundation’s holding; who actually holds the share is stated by OpenAI (cs-openai-foundation-elects-pbc-directors), not by this provision.

parties.actor: Holder of the Class N Common Stock (OpenAI Foundation)

subject: openai-group-pbc-certificate-2025

object.value: Class N holder’s prior written approval for five kinds of action

statement: The certificate states that, so long as Class N Common Stock is issued, outstanding and held by OpenAI Foundation, the prior written approval of its holder is required for the corporation to amend Article III (Public Benefit); to agree to or complete a deemed liquidation event or a sale of material assets of the corporation and its subsidiaries taken as a whole; to issue more Class N stock; to create or issue other stock entitled to vote on directors, except Class B stock in acquisitions; or to modify the certificate or bylaws in a way that disproportionately and adversely affects the Class N holder.

time.note: The certificate’s filing date, recorded as its publication date.

qualification: What the filed text says. The Delaware Attorney General’s statement records OpenAI’s representation of the same approval rights plus a sixth, over amendments to the PBC’s Corporate Governance Guidelines, “as further described in definitive documents”, which were not inspected (context below).

parties.actor: Holder of the Class N Common Stock

subject: openai-group-pbc-certificate-2025

object.value: Removal of directors by the Class N holder or by two-thirds of other stockholders

statement: The certificate states that directors may be removed with or without cause either by the vote of the holder of the Class N Common Stock, so long as any Class N shares are outstanding, or by holders of two-thirds of the voting power of the other capital stock voting as one class, in which case no more than one-third of the board may be removed in any twelve-month period.

time.note: The certificate’s filing date, recorded as its publication date.

qualification: What the filed text says. The same section provides that vacancies are filled by a majority vote of the stock entitled to vote on director elections, which it describes as initially controlled by the holder of the Class N stock.

parties.actor: Holder of the Class N Common Stock
Holders of two-thirds of the voting power excluding Class N (at most one-third of the board in twelve months)

subject: openai-group-pbc-certificate-2025

object.value: Board considers only the Mission on safety and security issues

time.note: The certificate’s filing date, recorded as its publication date.

subject: rsp-v3-0
statement: Whether RSP v3.0’s new roadmap and transparency mechanisms compensate for its reduced unilateral commitments, in the policy’s overall capacity to secure risk mitigation, remains unsettled.

time.note: v3.0’s effective date; the assessments were published on and after that date.

qualification: Unresolved open question, not a finding; it keeps the strength of the commitments apart from their expected effectiveness. Both sides accept the main changes: v3.0 drops the implied unilateral commitment to pause development and deployment when required safeguards cannot be met, separates recommendations for the industry from what Anthropic commits to as a company, adds transparency commitments, and introduces roadmap goals that are public goals rather than hard commitments. TIME’s report judges that overall the change leaves Anthropic far less constrained by its own safety policies. Sophie Williams and Jonas Freund, writing on GovAI’s site in a post that represents their own views, judge that it weakened future security commitments, note that existing mitigations are not lowered and conclude on balance that honesty about constraints is better than commitments that would not be followed; their article was updated on 2026-03-17 on competitor-matching commitments, and the quoted passages are unchanged. Anthropic describes the revision as amplifying what worked and committing it to more transparency. Holden Karnofsky, who led the revision and writes in his own name, expects more specific and realistic goals to improve their forcing function despite weaker consequences for missing them, and leaves the net effect uncertain. Jared Kaplan, Anthropic’s chief science officer, told TIME that unilateral commitments made no sense while competitors pressed ahead, and denied that the change was a U-turn or a capitulation to market incentives. METR’s Chris Painter, who reviewed an early draft with Anthropic’s permission, called the change understandable but was concerned it might enable a gradual “frog-boiling” effect. None of these passages settles whether the new mechanisms compensate, so all are context. The textual changes are recorded separately, and the record does not decide the question.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Anonymous internal disclosure process with monthly status updates to the discloser and at-least-quarterly sharing with officers and directors

statement: SB 53 requires a large frontier developer to provide a reasonable internal process through which a covered employee may anonymously disclose information the employee believes in good faith shows a specific and substantial danger to public health or safety resulting from a catastrophic risk, or a violation of the Act (Bus. & Prof. Code ch. 25.1). The process must give the discloser a monthly update on the investigation and actions taken, and disclosures and responses must be shared with the developer's officers and directors at least quarterly, except an officer or director whose wrongdoing is alleged.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29: approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State that day (Chapter 138, Statutes of 2025). The chaptered text states no effective date and contains no urgency clause, so this record does not establish an effective date.

qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. This is a statutory requirement only. It is not evidence that any developer has set up or operates such a process. 'Covered employee' has a narrow definition: an employee responsible for assessing, managing, or addressing risk of critical safety incidents (Lab. Code § 1107(b)). The provision therefore does not cover all employees. The applicability of the separate Lab. Code § 1102.5 protections to other employees is not addressed here. Framework texts that describe similar internal reporting channels are not evidence that they respond to this provision unless they say so explicitly.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Civil penalties under § 22757.15 recoverable only in a civil action brought by the Attorney General

statement: SB 53 provides that a civil penalty described in Bus. & Prof. Code § 22757.15 can be recovered only in a civil action brought by the California Attorney General.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29; the Governor approved it and it was filed with the Secretary of State that day. Effective 2026-01-01 according to the history note of codified Bus. & Prof. Code § 22757.15, which listed no amendment when checked on 2026-10-04.

qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. The Attorney General-only rule is limited to penalties described in § 22757.15. On the grounds listed in § 22757.15(a), that section makes a large frontier developer subject to a civil penalty whose amount depends on the severity of the violation and does not exceed $1,000,000 per violation. The party role 'decides' records only that the Attorney General alone may bring the civil action through which such a penalty is recovered. It does not mean that the Attorney General imposes or sets the penalty. Lab. Code § 1107.1(f)–(i), added by the same act, separately refers to civil actions and administrative proceedings 'brought pursuant to this section'. It authorises attorney's fees for a plaintiff who brings a successful action (f), sets a burden-of-proof rule (g), lets a covered employee petition the superior court for temporary or preliminary injunctive relief (h), and bars a stay of that relief pending appeal (i). Who may bring such actions is not resolved here (see stops). No enforcement action is recorded.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Catastrophic risk: death of or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage or loss, from a single incident

statement: SB 53 defines 'catastrophic risk' as a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier developer's development, storage, use or deployment of a frontier model will materially contribute to the death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or to more than $1 billion in damage to, or loss of, property, arising from a single incident in which a frontier model (a) provides expert-level assistance in creating or releasing a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon; (b) engages without meaningful human oversight in a cyberattack or in conduct that would be murder, assault, extortion or theft if committed by a human; or (c) evades the control of its developer or user. Stated exclusions apply.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Approved by the Governor and filed with the Secretary of State on 2025-09-29, per the chaptered bill header. The history note on codified § 22757.11 gives an effective date of 2026-01-01 (separate evidence item). The chaptered bill text states no effective date for Chapter 25.1.

qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. Exclusions (§ 22757.11(c)(2)): information a frontier model outputs that is otherwise publicly accessible in substantially similar form from a source other than a foundation model; lawful activity of the federal government; and harm from a frontier model combined with other software where the model did not materially contribute. subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Civil penalty up to $1,000,000 per violation

statement: Under SB 53, a large frontier developer that fails to publish or transmit a required compliant document, makes a statement prohibited by § 22757.12(e), fails to report an incident as required, or fails to comply with its own frontier AI framework is subject to a civil penalty. The penalty depends on the severity of the violation and may not exceed $1,000,000 per violation.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Critical safety incident report to OES within 15 days of discovery

statement: SB 53 requires a frontier developer to report any critical safety incident involving one or more of its frontier models to the Office of Emergency Services within 15 days of discovering it.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29. Effective 2026-01-01 according to the codified section's history note, 'Effective January 1, 2026' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=22757.13, checked 2026-10-04), which shows no amendment. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. § 22757.13(c)(1) is expressly 'subject to paragraph (2)', the 24-hour imminent-risk disclosure (separate record). How the two duties relate is a question of legal interpretation and is not recorded here. Under § 22757.13(h)–(i), OES may adopt regulations designating federal laws, regulations or guidance documents whose incident-reporting standards are substantially equivalent to, or stricter than, this section's. A frontier developer that declares to OES its intent to comply through such a designated standard is deemed in compliance with § 22757.13 to the extent it meets that standard (separate record). This record does not establish that any designation or declaration exists. A developer that later discovers information about an incident may file an amended report (§ 22757.13(c)(3)). Reporting critical safety incidents involving foundation models that are not frontier models is encouraged, not required (§ 22757.13(c)(4)). Critical safety incident reports submitted to OES under § 22757.13 are exempt from the California Public Records Act (§ 22757.13(f)). subject: california-sb-53

object.value: No materially false or misleading statements about framework implementation or compliance

statement: SB 53 prohibits a large frontier developer from making a materially false or misleading statement about its implementation of, or compliance with, its frontier AI framework. It also prohibits any frontier developer from making a materially false or misleading statement about catastrophic risk from its frontier models or about its management of catastrophic risk. The prohibition does not apply to a statement made in good faith that was reasonable under the circumstances.

qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. Subdivision (e)(1)(B) concerns statements about a large frontier developer's implementation of, or compliance with, its own frontier AI framework. Subdivision (e)(1)(A) concerns statements by any frontier developer about catastrophic risk from its frontier models or its management of catastrophic risk. Two questions are listed as stops and not resolved here because they need legal interpretation. The first is whether subdivision (e) reaches any named developer's published statement, for example the sentence asserting TFAIA compliance in xAI's December 2025 FAIF (record faif-2026-compliance-sentence). The second is whether that developer is a large frontier developer. A statement in violation of subdivision (e) is one of the grounds on which § 22757.15(a) makes a large frontier developer subject to a civil penalty. This record states what the statute requires. It says nothing about any developer's compliance.

A frontier developer that declares to OES its intent to comply through a designated federal standard is deemed in compliance with § 22757.13 to the extent it meets that standard, until it revokes the declaration or OES revokes the regulation; failing to meet the designated standard is a violation of the chapter.

object.value: Frontier developer: has trained or initiated training of a frontier model

statement: SB 53 defines a 'frontier developer' as a person who has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model, where that person has used or intends to use at least as much computing power to train it as the frontier-model definition specifies.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29; effective 2026-01-01. Codified § 22757.11, checked live on 2026-10-04, shows no amendment note.

qualification:
What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. A definition only. Whether a named company is a frontier developer is a question of legal application and is not recorded (see stops).

By their text, the following provisions are addressed to frontier developers: the basic transparency report (§ 22757.12(c)(1)); the bar on materially false or misleading statements about catastrophic risk (§ 22757.12(e)(1)(A)); critical-safety-incident reporting (§ 22757.13(c)); and the whistleblower prohibitions and notice duty (Lab. Code § 1107.1(a), (b) and (d)).

The following are addressed only to large frontier developers: the frontier AI framework (§ 22757.12(a)–(b)); the catastrophic-risk summaries in the transparency report (§ 22757.12(c)(2)); internal-use assessment summaries to the Office of Emergency Services (§ 22757.12(d)); the bar on false statements about framework implementation or compliance (§ 22757.12(e)(1)(B)); and the anonymous internal disclosure process (Lab. Code § 1107.1(e)).

The civil-penalty provision (§ 22757.15(a)) names only large frontier developers. This record does not interpret enforcement or applicability beyond the text.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Frontier model: foundation model trained with more than 10^26 operations

statement: SB 53 defines a 'frontier model' as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations. The count includes the original training run and any later fine-tuning, reinforcement learning or other material modifications that the developer applies to a preceding foundation model.

time.note: Provision as stated in the chaptered text published and approved on 2025-09-29; the added sections took effect on 2026-01-01. Text as chaptered on 2025-09-29; effective 2026-01-01. A definition only: it does not establish which models or developers meet it. Section 22757.14(a) requires the Department of Technology, on or before 1 January 2027 and annually thereafter, to assess recent evidence and developments and recommend whether and how to update this definition, along with the 'frontier developer' and 'large frontier developer' definitions. Section 22757.14(c) requires it to submit a report with those recommendations to the Legislature. This record does not interpret who may amend the definition or what legal effect the recommendations have.

subject: california-sb-53

object.value: Internal-use catastrophic-risk assessment summaries to OES every three months or on another reasonable schedule

statement: SB 53 requires a large frontier developer to transmit to the Office of Emergency Services a summary of any assessment of catastrophic risk resulting from internal use of its frontier models. The summary is due every three months, or on another reasonable schedule that the developer specifies and communicates to OES in writing, with written updates as appropriate.

It must also take all necessary precautions to limit access to reports on internal use to personnel with a specific need to know (§ 22757.13(b)(1)–(2)). Reports of assessments of catastrophic risk from internal use are exempt from the California Public Records Act (§ 22757.13(f)). A statutory duty is not evidence that any summary has been transmitted.

statement: SB 53 requires a frontier developer, before or at the same time as deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model, to publish clearly and conspicuously on its website a transparency report with listed basic information. A large frontier developer must also include summaries of its catastrophic-risk assessments under its frontier AI framework, their results, the extent of third-party evaluator involvement, and other steps taken to fulfil its framework for that model.

qualification: What the enacted text states, quoted from the chaptered expression. It is not evidence that the statute applies to any named developer, or of compliance, enforcement or effect. 'Deploy' means making a frontier model available to a third party for use, modification, copying or combination with other software. It excludes making the model available to a third party for the primary purpose of developing or evaluating it (§ 22757.11(e)). The statute does not define 'substantially modified'. A large frontier developer's framework must describe how it decides when its models are substantially modified enough to require these disclosures (§ 22757.12(a)(6)). Publishing the information as part of a larger document, including a system card or model card, is deemed compliance with the applicable paragraph (§ 22757.12(c)(3)). A frontier developer is encouraged, but not required, to make these disclosures consistent with, or superior to, industry best practices (§ 22757.12(c)(4)). Published documents may be redacted where necessary to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety or US national security, or to comply with federal or state law. The developer must describe the character and justification of each redaction, to the extent those concerns permit, and keep the unredacted information for five years (§ 22757.12(f)). A statutory requirement is not evidence that any report was published, or that any report was complete or adequate.
